Concept Tested: Canonical Normal Forms (PDNF Minterms / PCNF Maxterms) and Truth-Assignment Counting
(‘DM.1.1‘).



Formula / Principle: For a formula F over n variables, the number of minterms in its PDNF equals the number of
truth assignments satisfying F(v) = T, while the number of maxterms in its PCNF equals the number of falsifying
assignments F(v) = F, with Minterms(F) + Maxterms(F) = 2n = 16.
Step-by-Step Reasoning: For 4 variables (p1, p2, p3, p4), the sub-formula (p1 →p2) is false only when (p1, p2) =
(T, F), leaving 4 −1 = 3 satisfying pairs. Independently, (p3 ∨p4) is false only when (p3, p4) = (F, F), leaving
4 −1 = 3 satisfying pairs. By the product rule, the number of satisfying truth assignments (and thus minterms in the
PDNF) is 3 × 3 = 9.
Common Mistake: Forgetting to account for all 4 variables or confusing PDNF minterm counts (True rows) with
PCNF maxterm counts (False rows).

assignments F(v) = F, with Minterms(F) + Maxterms(F) = 2n = 32.

of 23 = 8 assignments), so it holds for 8 −1 = 7 assignments. Thus, the total number of minterms in its PDNF is
2 × 7 = 14.

PCNF maxterm counts (False rows).

the unique M-optimal (and simultaneously W-pessimal) stable matching µM ∈S, in which every proposer
m ∈M is matched to their most-preferred partner achievable in ANY stable matching.

By Conway’s and Knuth’s Distributive Lattice Theorem, under the dominance partial order (µ ⪯µ′ iff every
m ∈M weakly prefers µ(m) to µ′(m)), the set of all stable matchings (S, ⪯) forms a finite distributive lattice
where the meet and join are obtained by taking the pointwise best and worst partners for M (and worst/best
for W).

Making the M-proposing Gale-Shapley mechanism is strategy-proof (truthful) for all proposers in M: no
single proposer m ∈M can ever obtain a strictly better partner by misreporting their preference list (Dubins-
Freedman 1981 / Roth 1982).

In every instance, the M-proposing and W-proposing Gale-Shapley algorithms always produce the exact same
matching.

assigning each m ∈M the better (or worse) of µ(m), µ′(m) is again a bijection and a stable matching, making (S, ⪯)
a finite distributive lattice (and by Birkhoff’s representation theorem, every finite distributive lattice arises as the
stable matching lattice of some instance!). - Option C (TRUE): By the Dubins-Freedman / Roth theorem, truthful
reporting is a dominant strategy for the proposing side M. - Option D (FALSE): µM = µW holds only when the

question:
Consider an instance of the Gale-Shapley Stable Matching Problem (1962) with n = 7 proposers (Set M) and
n = 7 reviewers (Set W), where every agent has a strict total preference ordering over all n members of the opposite
side. Which of the following fundamental properties of the set S of all stable matchings is/are ALWAYS TRUE?
options:
The Gale-Shapley algorithm where M proposes terminates in at most n2 −n + 1 proposals and always outputs
the unique M-optimal (and simultaneously W-pessimal) stable matching µM ∈S, in which every proposer
m ∈M is matched to their most-preferred partner achievable in ANY stable matching.

By Conway’s and Knuth’s Distributive Lattice Theorem, under the dominance partial order (µ ⪯µ′ iff every
m ∈M weakly prefers µ(m) to µ′(m)), the set of all stable matchings (S, ⪯) forms a finite distributive lattice
where the meet and join are obtained by taking the pointwise best and worst partners for M (and worst/best
for W).

Making the M-proposing Gale-Shapley mechanism is strategy-proof (truthful) for all proposers in M: no
single proposer m ∈M can ever obtain a strictly better partner by misreporting their preference list (Dubins-
Freedman 1981 / Roth 1982).

In every instance, the M-proposing and W-proposing Gale-Shapley algorithms always produce the exact same
matching.

the unique M-optimal (and simultaneously W-pessimal) stable matching µM ∈S, in which every proposer
m ∈M is matched to their most-preferred partner achievable in ANY stable matching.

By Conway’s and Knuth’s Distributive Lattice Theorem, under the dominance partial order (µ ⪯µ′ iff every
m ∈M weakly prefers µ(m) to µ′(m)), the set of all stable matchings (S, ⪯) forms a finite distributive lattice
where the meet and join are obtained by taking the pointwise best and worst partners for M (and worst/best
for W).

single proposer m ∈M can ever obtain a strictly better partner by misreporting their preference list (Dubins-
Freedman 1981 / Roth 1982).

By Conway’s and Knuth’s Distributive Lattice Theorem, under the dominance partial order (µ ⪯µ′ iff every
m ∈M weakly prefers µ(m) to µ′(m)), the set of all stable matchings (S, ⪯) forms a finite distributive lattice

the unique M-optimal (and simultaneously W-pessimal) stable matching µM ∈S, in which every proposer
m ∈M is matched to their most-preferred partner achievable in ANY stable matching.

By Conway’s and Knuth’s Distributive Lattice Theorem, under the dominance partial order (µ ⪯µ′ iff every
m ∈M weakly prefers µ(m) to µ′(m)), the set of all stable matchings (S, ⪯) forms a finite distributive lattice
where the meet and join are obtained by taking the pointwise best and worst partners for M (and worst/best
for W).

Making the M-proposing Gale-Shapley mechanism is strategy-proof (truthful) for all proposers in M: no
single proposer m ∈M can ever obtain a strictly better partner by misreporting their preference list (Dubins-
Freedman 1981 / Roth 1982).

In every instance, the M-proposing and W-proposing Gale-Shapley algorithms always produce the exact same
matching.

to O(n2) by Kawarabayashi-Kobayashi-Reed 2012). - Option C (TRUE): Hadwiger’s Conjecture holds for t ≤6

nor topological minor is a WQO. Correct options: A, B, C.
question:
In topological and structural graph theory (test variant 1), a graph H is a minor of G (H ⪯m G) if H can be obtained
from a subgraph of G by contracting edges, and H is a topological minor (subdivision) of G if a subdivision of H
is a subgraph of G. Which of the following theorems and conjectures is/are ALWAYS TRUE?
options:
While K5 and K3,3 are both minors and topological minors for planarity (Kuratowski’s Theorem 1930 /
Wagner’s Theorem 1937), in general H ⪯m G does NOT imply that G contains a subdivision of H (for
example, the Petersen graph contains K5 as a minor by contracting the 5 spoke matching edges, yet has
maximum degree 3 and therefore contains NO subdivision of K5, though when ∆(H) ≤3, H is a minor of G if
and only if H is a topological minor of G!).

By the Robertson-Seymour Graph Minor Theorem (1983-2004, Graph Minors I-XX), the class of all finite
graphs is well-quasi-ordered (WQO) by the graph minor relation ⪯m (there is no infinite antichain of graphs
under ⪯m); consequently, every minor-closed graph property P is characterized by a finite set of forbidden
minors F(P) and can be tested in O(n3) polynomial time!

Hadwiger’s Conjecture (1943) states that if χ(G) ≥t, then G contains Kt as a minor; this has been proved
to be TRUE for all 1 ≤t ≤6 (where t ≤4 was proved by Hadwiger/Dirac without the Four-Color Theorem,
t = 5 was proved equivalent to the Four-Color Theorem by Wagner 1937, and t = 6 was proved equivalent to
the Four-Color Theorem by Robertson, Seymour, and Thomas in 1993!).
Subgraph isomorphism is a well-quasi-ordering on the set of all finite simple graphs.

Analysis of Options: - Option A (TRUE): Contracting the 5 spoke edges of the Petersen graph yields K5, while a
subdivision of K5 requires 5 vertices of degree ≥4; for ∆(H) ≤3, vertex splitting reverses edge contraction so minor
and topological minor coincide. - Option B (TRUE): Robertson and Seymour’s 20-paper series proved Wagner’s
Conjecture (WQO under minors) and gave an O(n3) algorithm for testing any fixed minor H ⪯m G (improved
to O(n2) by Kawarabayashi-Kobayashi-Reed 2012). - Option C (TRUE): Hadwiger’s Conjecture holds for t ≤6
(Robertson-Seymour-Thomas 1993) and remains open for t ≥7. - Option D (FALSE): The infinite sequence of cycles
C3, C4, C5, C6, . . . is an infinite antichain under the subgraph (and topological minor!) relation, so neither subgraph
nor topological minor is a WQO. Correct options: A, B, C.
question:
In topological and structural graph theory (test variant 2), a graph H is a minor of G (H ⪯m G) if H can be obtained
from a subgraph of G by contracting edges, and H is a topological minor (subdivision) of G if a subdivision of H
is a subgraph of G. Which of the following theorems and conjectures is/are ALWAYS TRUE?
options:
While K5 and K3,3 are both minors and topological minors for planarity (Kuratowski’s Theorem 1930 /
Wagner’s Theorem 1937), in general H ⪯m G does NOT imply that G contains a subdivision of H (for
example, the Petersen graph contains K5 as a minor by contracting the 5 spoke matching edges, yet has
maximum degree 3 and therefore contains NO subdivision of K5, though when ∆(H) ≤3, H is a minor of G if
and only if H is a topological minor of G!).

By the Robertson-Seymour Graph Minor Theorem (1983-2004, Graph Minors I-XX), the class of all finite
graphs is well-quasi-ordered (WQO) by the graph minor relation ⪯m (there is no infinite antichain of graphs
under ⪯m); consequently, every minor-closed graph property P is characterized by a finite set of forbidden
minors F(P) and can be tested in O(n3) polynomial time!

Hadwiger’s Conjecture (1943) states that if χ(G) ≥t, then G contains Kt as a minor; this has been proved
to be TRUE for all 1 ≤t ≤6 (where t ≤4 was proved by Hadwiger/Dirac without the Four-Color Theorem,
t = 5 was proved equivalent to the Four-Color Theorem by Wagner 1937, and t = 6 was proved equivalent to
the Four-Color Theorem by Robertson, Seymour, and Thomas in 1993!).
Subgraph isomorphism is a well-quasi-ordering on the set of all finite simple graphs.

question:
In topological and structural graph theory (test variant 3), a graph H is a minor of G (H ⪯m G) if H can be obtained
from a subgraph of G by contracting edges, and H is a topological minor (subdivision) of G if a subdivision of H
is a subgraph of G. Which of the following theorems and conjectures is/are ALWAYS TRUE?
options:
While K5 and K3,3 are both minors and topological minors for planarity (Kuratowski’s Theorem 1930 /
Wagner’s Theorem 1937), in general H ⪯m G does NOT imply that G contains a subdivision of H (for
example, the Petersen graph contains K5 as a minor by contracting the 5 spoke matching edges, yet has
maximum degree 3 and therefore contains NO subdivision of K5, though when ∆(H) ≤3, H is a minor of G if
and only if H is a topological minor of G!).

By the Robertson-Seymour Graph Minor Theorem (1983-2004, Graph Minors I-XX), the class of all finite
graphs is well-quasi-ordered (WQO) by the graph minor relation ⪯m (there is no infinite antichain of graphs
under ⪯m); consequently, every minor-closed graph property P is characterized by a finite set of forbidden
minors F(P) and can be tested in O(n3) polynomial time!

Hadwiger’s Conjecture (1943) states that if χ(G) ≥t, then G contains Kt as a minor; this has been proved
to be TRUE for all 1 ≤t ≤6 (where t ≤4 was proved by Hadwiger/Dirac without the Four-Color Theorem,
t = 5 was proved equivalent to the Four-Color Theorem by Wagner 1937, and t = 6 was proved equivalent to
the Four-Color Theorem by Robertson, Seymour, and Thomas in 1993!).
Subgraph isomorphism is a well-quasi-ordering on the set of all finite simple graphs.

(ruling out B and C), and wreath products of aperiodic monoids are always aperiodic (ruling out D). Thus A is
uniquely correct.

Using character theory (or Goldschmidt-Bender-Matsuyama group-theoretic proofs), |G| = paqb =⇒G is solvable.
2. Feit-Thompson (1963): Every group of odd order is solvable; hence any non-abelian simple group has even order

Thompson refutes C; S3 (order 6) and S4 (order 24) are non-abelian solvable groups (ruling out D). Thus A is
uniquely correct.

options:
By Craig’s Interpolation Theorem, if φ and ψ are first-order sentences (with equality) such that φ |= ψ, then
there exists a first-order sentence θ (the Craig interpolant) such that φ |= θ and θ |= ψ, and every non-logical
symbol (predicate, function, or constant) occurring in θ occurs in BOTH φ and ψ.

By Lyndon’s Interpolation Theorem, the interpolant θ can be chosen so that every predicate symbol P occur-
ring positively (respectively, negatively) in θ occurs positively (respectively, negatively) in both φ and ψ; as a
corollary, a first-order sentence χ is preserved under surjective homomorphisms if and only if χ is logically
equivalent to a positive sentence (built using ∧, ∨, ∀, ∃, = without ¬).

By Beth’s Definability Theorem (which is a direct consequence of Craig’s Interpolation Theorem), in First-
Order Logic, a new k-ary predicate symbol R is implicitly defined by a theory T(σ ∪{R}) (meaning any
two expansions (M, R1), (M, R2) |= T of the same σ-structure satisfy R1 = R2) if and only if R is explicitly
definable in T by a first-order σ-formula δ(x1, . . . , xk): T |= ∀⃗x (R(⃗x) ↔δ(⃗x)).

Craig’s Interpolation Theorem continues to hold when restricted strictly to finite structures (Finite Model The-

from a subgraph of G by contracting edges, and H is a topological minor (subdivision) of G if a subdivision of H
is a subgraph of G. Which of the following theorems and conjectures is/are ALWAYS TRUE?
options:

Wagner’s Theorem 1937), in general H ⪯m G does NOT imply that G contains a subdivision of H (for
example, the Petersen graph contains K5 as a minor by contracting the 5 spoke matching edges, yet has
maximum degree 3 and therefore contains NO subdivision of K5, though when ∆(H) ≤3, H is a minor of G if
and only if H is a topological minor of G!).

By the Robertson-Seymour Graph Minor Theorem (1983-2004, Graph Minors I-XX), the class of all finite
graphs is well-quasi-ordered (WQO) by the graph minor relation ⪯m (there is no infinite antichain of graphs
under ⪯m); consequently, every minor-closed graph property P is characterized by a finite set of forbidden
minors F(P) and can be tested in O(n3) polynomial time!

to be TRUE for all 1 ≤t ≤6 (where t ≤4 was proved by Hadwiger/Dirac without the Four-Color Theorem,
t = 5 was proved equivalent to the Four-Color Theorem by Wagner 1937, and t = 6 was proved equivalent to
the Four-Color Theorem by Robertson, Seymour, and Thomas in 1993!).
Subgraph isomorphism is a well-quasi-ordering on the set of all finite simple graphs.

minimum model), not OR (ruling out D). Thus A is uniquely correct.

cliques (Cu and Cv). 3. Whitney’s Theorem (1932): L(K3) ∼= K3 ∼= L(K1,3) is the unique pair of non-isomorphic
connected simple graphs with isomorphic line graphs!

are 9 minimal forbidden induced subgraphs (including K1,3, K5 −e, and the 6-vertex wheel W5, ruling out B);
Whitney’s Theorem rules out C; and since AL(G) = BT B −2I where B is the vertex-edge incidence matrix, the
minimum eigenvalue of L(G) is ≥−2 (not −1, ruling out D). Thus A is uniquely correct.

even degree 2k, every connected component of G has an Eulerian circuit. Orienting each Eulerian circuit gives a
directed graph D in which every vertex v ∈V (G) has d−(v) = d+(v) = k. 2. Construct a bipartite graph B with
parts (V +, V −) (two copies of V (G)) and an edge (u+, v−) for each directed edge (u, v) ∈E(D). Then B is a k-
regular bipartite graph! 3. By König’s / Hall’s Theorem, E(B) decomposes into k edge-disjoint perfect matchings
M1, . . . , Mk; contracting (v+, v−) back to v turns each Mi into a 2-regular spanning subgraph (a 2-factor) of G!
Method 2 (Elimination of B, C, D): The Petersen graph is 3-regular and bridgeless, so by Petersen’s 1-factor theorem
it has a 1-factor (and a complementary 2-factor C5 ⊔C5), but it is NOT 1-factorable (χ′(P) = 4, ruling out B, and
C5 ⊔C5 also shows a 2-factor can be a union of disjoint cycles rather than a single Hamiltonian cycle, ruling out D);
and K2n+1 has odd order so it has no 1-factor (instead K2n+1 is 2-factorable into n Hamiltonian cycles by Walecki’s
construction, while K2n is 1-factorable into 2n −1 perfect matchings, ruling out C). Thus A is uniquely correct.

Method 1 (Lewis’s 2-SAT Reduction for Renameable-Horn): Introduce a boolean renaming variable ri ∈{0, 1}
for each variable xi, where ri = 1 means xi is flipped. After renaming, a clause C = (ℓ1 ∨· · · ∨ℓk) is Horn iff
it contains at most one positive literal, which is equivalent to requiring that for every pair of literals ℓa, ℓb ∈C
(a < b), ¬(pos(ℓa) ∧pos(ℓb)) = (¬pos(ℓa) ∨¬pos(ℓb)) – a 2-CNF clause! Using the linear-time encoding of at-most-
one constraints, testing whether Φ is renameable-Horn (and solving it via Dowling-Gallier forward chaining) takes
O(∥Φ∥) time!
Method 2 (Elimination of B, C, D): Renameable-Horn recognition is in P (ruling out B); (x1 ∨x2) has two positive
literals so it is not Horn without renaming (ruling out C); and Horn formulas are closed under bitwise AND (unique
minimum model), not OR (ruling out D). Thus A is uniquely correct.

are 9 minimal forbidden induced subgraphs (including K1,3, K5 −e, and the 6-vertex wheel W5, ruling out B);
Whitney’s Theorem rules out C; and since AL(G) = BT B −2I where B is the vertex-edge incidence matrix, the
minimum eigenvalue of L(G) is ≥−2 (not −1, ruling out D). Thus A is uniquely correct.

even degree 2k, every connected component of G has an Eulerian circuit. Orienting each Eulerian circuit gives a
directed graph D in which every vertex v ∈V (G) has d−(v) = d+(v) = k. 2. Construct a bipartite graph B with

M1, . . . , Mk; contracting (v+, v−) back to v turns each Mi into a 2-regular spanning subgraph (a 2-factor) of G!

C5 ⊔C5 also shows a 2-factor can be a union of disjoint cycles rather than a single Hamiltonian cycle, ruling out D);

construction, while K2n is 1-factorable into 2n −1 perfect matchings, ruling out C). Thus A is uniquely correct.

and m edges (test variant 2). Which of the following statements are ALWAYS TRUE?
options:
Dirac’s Theorem (1961) & Rose-Tarjan-Lueker (1976): The following are equivalent for a graph G: (1) G
is chordal (every cycle of length ≥4 has a chord); (2) every minimal vertex separator of G is a clique; (3)
every induced subgraph of G has a simplicial vertex (whose neighborhood is a clique), so G admits a Perfect
Elimination Ordering (PEO) computable in O(n+m) time via Lexicographic Breadth-First Search (LexBFS)
or Maximum Cardinality Search (MCS)!

Gavril’s Subtree Intersection Theorem (1974): A graph G is chordal if and only if G is the intersection graph
of a family of subtrees of a tree T (specifically, the clique tree of G whose nodes are the maximal cliques of G,
of which a chordal graph on n vertices has at most n maximal cliques)!

Lekkerkerker-Boland Theorem (1962) & Gilmore-Hoffman Theorem (1964): A graph G is an interval
graph (intersection graph of intervals on the real line) if and only if G is chordal and asteroidal-triple-free
(AT-free), which holds if and only if G is chordal and its complement G is a comparability graph!

for each variable xi, where ri = 1 means xi is flipped. After renaming, a clause C = (ℓ1 ∨· · · ∨ℓk) is Horn iff
it contains at most one positive literal, which is equivalent to requiring that for every pair of literals ℓa, ℓb ∈C

literals so it is not Horn without renaming (ruling out C); and Horn formulas are closed under bitwise AND (unique
minimum model), not OR (ruling out D). Thus A is uniquely correct.

even degree 2k, every connected component of G has an Eulerian circuit. Orienting each Eulerian circuit gives a
directed graph D in which every vertex v ∈V (G) has d−(v) = d+(v) = k. 2. Construct a bipartite graph B with
parts (V +, V −) (two copies of V (G)) and an edge (u+, v−) for each directed edge (u, v) ∈E(D). Then B is a k-
regular bipartite graph! 3. By König’s / Hall’s Theorem, E(B) decomposes into k edge-disjoint perfect matchings
M1, . . . , Mk; contracting (v+, v−) back to v turns each Mi into a 2-regular spanning subgraph (a 2-factor) of G!
Method 2 (Elimination of B, C, D): The Petersen graph is 3-regular and bridgeless, so by Petersen’s 1-factor theorem
it has a 1-factor (and a complementary 2-factor C5 ⊔C5), but it is NOT 1-factorable (χ′(P) = 4, ruling out B, and
C5 ⊔C5 also shows a 2-factor can be a union of disjoint cycles rather than a single Hamiltonian cycle, ruling out D);
and K2n+1 has odd order so it has no 1-factor (instead K2n+1 is 2-factorable into n Hamiltonian cycles by Walecki’s
construction, while K2n is 1-factorable into 2n −1 perfect matchings, ruling out C). Thus A is uniquely correct.

(1955): Given G = (V, E) with V = {v1, . . . , vn}, M(G) adds a shadow vertex ui for each vi (adjacent to NG(vi)) and

even degree 2k, every connected component of G has an Eulerian circuit. Orienting each Eulerian circuit gives a
directed graph D in which every vertex v ∈V (G) has d−(v) = d+(v) = k. 2. Construct a bipartite graph B with
parts (V +, V −) (two copies of V (G)) and an edge (u+, v−) for each directed edge (u, v) ∈E(D). Then B is a k-
regular bipartite graph! 3. By König’s / Hall’s Theorem, E(B) decomposes into k edge-disjoint perfect matchings
M1, . . . , Mk; contracting (v+, v−) back to v turns each Mi into a 2-regular spanning subgraph (a 2-factor) of G!
Method 2 (Elimination of B, C, D): The Petersen graph is 3-regular and bridgeless, so by Petersen’s 1-factor theorem
it has a 1-factor (and a complementary 2-factor C5 ⊔C5), but it is NOT 1-factorable (χ′(P) = 4, ruling out B, and
C5 ⊔C5 also shows a 2-factor can be a union of disjoint cycles rather than a single Hamiltonian cycle, ruling out D);
and K2n+1 has odd order so it has no 1-factor (instead K2n+1 is 2-factorable into n Hamiltonian cycles by Walecki’s
construction, while K2n is 1-factorable into 2n −1 perfect matchings, ruling out C). Thus A is uniquely correct.

for Boolean Algebras (1936), Birkhoff’s Representation Theorem for Finite Distributive Lattices (1937), and

options:
In any bounded distributive lattice L, a proper filter F ⊊L is a prime filter (x ∨y ∈F =⇒x ∈F or y ∈F) if
and only if its complement I = L \ F is a prime ideal (x ∧y ∈I =⇒x ∈I or y ∈I), which holds if and only
if the characteristic indicator map χF : L →{0, 1} is a bounded lattice homomorphism!

In a Boolean algebra B, the notions of prime filter and ultrafilter (maximal proper filter) coincide: for every
element a ∈B and every ultrafilter U ⊆B, exactly one of a ∈U or a ∈U holds

F ⊆L is a principal filter F = ↑p = {x ∈L : x ≥p} generated by a unique join-irreducible element
p ∈J (L), establishing an order-isomorphism between (J (L), ≤) and the poset of prime ideals ordered by
reverse inclusion (or prime filters ordered by inclusion)

Every countable Boolean algebra is isomorphic to a power-set algebra P(X) for some finite or countably infinite
set X

every induced subgraph of G has a simplicial vertex (whose neighborhood is a clique), so G admits a Perfect
Elimination Ordering (PEO) computable in O(n+m) time via Lexicographic Breadth-First Search (LexBFS)
or Maximum Cardinality Search (MCS)!

of a family of subtrees of a tree T (specifically, the clique tree of G whose nodes are the maximal cliques of G,
of which a chordal graph on n vertices has at most n maximal cliques)!

graph (intersection graph of intervals on the real line) if and only if G is chordal and asteroidal-triple-free
(AT-free), which holds if and only if G is chordal and its complement G is a comparability graph!

subject: Discrete Mathematics
explanation:
A
Method 1 (Grötzsch’s Theorem vs Mycielski’s Triangle-Free Chromatic Construction): 1. Grötzsch’s Theorem
(1959): Every planar graph containing no K3 is properly 3-vertex-colorable (χ(G) ≤3). 2. Mycielski’s Construction
(1955): Given G = (V, E) with V = {v1, . . . , vn}, M(G) adds a shadow vertex ui for each vi (adjacent to NG(vi)) and
a universal apex w adjacent to {u1, . . . , un}. - Vertices: |V (M(G))| = 2n + 1. - Edges: |E(M(G))| = |E| + 2|E| + n =
3m + n. - Since {u1, . . . , un} is an independent set, w is in no triangle, and if G is triangle-free then M(G) is triangle-
free with χ(M(G)) = χ(G) + 1! - Starting from M2 = K2 (n = 2, m = 1, χ = 2) gives M3 = C5 (n = 5, m = 5, χ = 3)
and the Grötzsch graph M4 = M(C5) (n = 2(5)+1 = 11 vertices, m = 3(5)+5 = 20 edges, triangle-free with χ = 4,
hence non-planar by Grötzsch’s Theorem!).
Method 2 (Elimination of B, C, D): Mycielski’s graphs have ω = 2 and arbitrarily large χ (ruling out B and D); and
the planar graph C4 with a subdivided chord (or a planar graph containing C5) has girth ≥4 (or 5) and χ = 3 (ruling
out C). Thus A is uniquely correct.

Method 1 (p-Adic Analytic Method of Skolem, Mahler & Lech): 1. Skolem-Mahler-Lech Theorem: Embedding
the characteristic roots and coefficients into a p-adic field Qp where the roots are p-adic units and applying Strass-
mann’s Theorem (every non-zero p-adic power series on Zp has at most finitely many zeros in Zp) on each residue
class modulo d = p −1 (or the multiplicative order mod p) proves that in each arithmetic progression r + md, either
ar+md = 0 for all m or ar+md = 0 for only finitely many m! 2. Non-Degenerate Case: If no ratio λi/λj (iej) is a
root of unity, no full arithmetic progression can vanish unless an ≡0, so |Z(a)| < ∞!
Method 2 (Elimination of B, C, D): Neither primes nor squares are a union of a finite set and arithmetic progressions
(ruling out B); a periodic sequence like an = 1 −(−1)n (an = an−2) has infinitely many zeros along the arithmetic
progression 2N (ruling out C); and decidability of the Skolem Problem for arbitrary order k ≥5 remains one of
the most famous open problems in theoretical computer science (known decidable for k ≤4 by Mignotte-Shorey-
Tijdeman-Vereshchagin, ruling out D). Thus A is uniquely correct.

paths of length 2), the 3 leaves have distance 4 from each other and their neighbors form a cut-set in T 2, making T 2

question:

(test variant 5). Which of the following theorems on Hamiltonian cycles and graph powers are ALWAYS TRUE?
options:

adding an edge {u, v} between any pair of non-adjacent vertices satisfying deg(u) + deg(v) ≥n (until no such
pair remains) is uniquely defined (independent of the order in which edges are added), and G is Hamiltonian
if and only if cl(G) is Hamiltonian (in particular, if cl(G) = Kn, then G is Hamiltonian)!

Chvátal’s Degree Sequence Theorem (1972): If dk > k OR dn−k ≥n−k holds for every integer 1 ≤k < n/2,
then G is Hamiltonian (and this condition is the best possible monotone degree-sequence condition: if it fails
for some k < n/2, there exists a non-Hamiltonian graph whose degree sequence majorizes d)!

Fleischner’s Theorem (1974) & Sekanina-Karaganis Theorem (1960): For any 2-vertex-connected (bicon-
nected) graph G on n ≥3 vertices, its square graph G2 (connecting vertices at distance ≤2 in G) is always
Hamiltonian; and for any connected graph G on n ≥3 vertices, its cube graph G3 (connecting vertices at
distance ≤3) is always Hamiltonian (and in fact Hamilton-connected)!

and m edges (test variant 5). Which of the following statements are ALWAYS TRUE?

is chordal (every cycle of length ≥4 has a chord); (2) every minimal vertex separator of G is a clique; (3)
every induced subgraph of G has a simplicial vertex (whose neighborhood is a clique), so G admits a Perfect
Elimination Ordering (PEO) computable in O(n+m) time via Lexicographic Breadth-First Search (LexBFS)
or Maximum Cardinality Search (MCS)!

Gavril’s Subtree Intersection Theorem (1974): A graph G is chordal if and only if G is the intersection graph
of a family of subtrees of a tree T (specifically, the clique tree of G whose nodes are the maximal cliques of G,
of which a chordal graph on n vertices has at most n maximal cliques)!

Lekkerkerker-Boland Theorem (1962) & Gilmore-Hoffman Theorem (1964): A graph G is an interval
graph (intersection graph of intervals on the real line) if and only if G is chordal and asteroidal-triple-free
(AT-free), which holds if and only if G is chordal and its complement G is a comparability graph!

Every chordal graph is an interval graph (for example, the subdivided star S(K1,3) on 7 vertices is an interval
graph)
